summary:
Labuan is a federal territory of Malaysia and stands under the Malaysian national framework: sections 377A and 377B of the Penal Code 1936 criminalise "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" and acts of gross indecency, carrying up to 20 years' imprisonment and whipping. The provisions apply to any person regardless of gender or consent, are not confined to Malaysian nationals, and therefore reach foreign visitors in Labuan.

The Sharia layer that criminalises cross-dressing and "a man posing as a woman" applies to Muslims only, and a dual court system places Muslims under Sharia jurisdiction while the national courts handle Penal Code offences. A non-Muslim foreign visitor falls outside the Sharia offences; the federal provisions, which carry the heavier penalties and apply to everyone, are the operative exposure. The sources reviewed do not record the text of Labuan's own Sharia enactment on gender expression.

No legal gender-recognition procedure is recorded for Malaysia, so a visitor's passport and identity documents are unlikely to carry a changed gender marker. What happens when a traveller's marker does not match presentation at Labuan immigration or during a police check is not documented in the sources.

The recorded pattern of enforcement is raid-based arrest and public outing rather than individual stops against consenting adults in private, and tourists are rarely targeted. Since the 2018 election, police have raided an LGBT Halloween party in Kuala Lumpur in October 2022 with at least 20 people arrested, an LGBT venue in August with twenty men arrested, and on 28 November 2025 a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur, where 208 men were arrested under section 377B. In that operation 31 of those held were foreign nationals whose embassies intervened, and detainees' faces and personal details were leaked after media had been pre-tipped.

Trans people in Malaysia face lethal violence and official indifference to it. A transgender woman was killed in Klang on 25 June 2019, the third killing of a trans woman in the country in fewer than two months; documentation of that case records police mistreatment and impunity.
tangentialFactors:
Malaysia criminalises sodomy and same-sex conduct at federal level since 1871, and every one of the 13 states plus the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya maintains Sharia enactments reaching cross-dressing; the state layer has been narrowed by litigation without loosening the federal one. The High Court denied a request to declare the Sharia cross-dressing prohibition unconstitutional, and the Federal Court struck down Selangor's section 28 in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024 on division-of-powers grounds, leaving Penal Code offences fully intact. A constitutional challenge was pending as of late 2014 following the mass arrest of 16 trans women at a wedding on 8 June 2014.

Official hostility has been stated in explicit terms. In July 2020 the Religious Affairs Minister announced that the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi) had his "full licence to carry out its enforcement actions" against transgender persons, an order the International Commission of Jurists demanded be revoked. In the Nur Sajat case, 122 religious officers were mobilised to pursue her for "inspecting Islam" before she fled to Thailand and received UNHCR protection.

Political turbulence around the federal provisions continued into December 2025: on 2 December the Home Minister floated revisiting them, and days later police raided another sauna in Penang.

Human Rights Watch and Justice For Sisters published a report on conversion practices, discrimination and violence on 10 August 2022, drawing on interviews with 73 LGBT people across Malaysia between 2018 and 2021. Islamist opposition has foreclosed reform prospects, LGBT events and media content are censored, and no same-sex marriage or anti-discrimination law exists.
localsOnly:
The Sharia offences that reach cross-dressing and "a man posing as a woman" apply to Muslims only. Since the 1980s all 13 states have passed such enactments, carrying up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning, and three of them also bar women from posing as men. Enforcement is carried out by state Islamic religious departments, and the laws contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing.

No legal gender-recognition procedure is recorded, so residents cannot obtain documents matching their lived gender. There is no anti-discrimination law and no same-sex marriage.

Government-funded mukhayyam "rehabilitation" retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021. In November 2023 Johor announced plans for conversion-therapy centres, and a Terengganu Sharia court ordered a lesbian couple caned.

Violence against transgender residents is documented with official indifference attached: the killing of a transgender woman in Klang on 25 June 2019 was the third such killing in fewer than two months, and the case file is documented under the heading "The Deceased Can't Speak for Herself", recording police mistreatment and impunity.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Labuan-specific enforcement case appears in the sources reviewed; every raid, arrest and killing cited here is documented in Kuala Lumpur, Penang, Johor, Terengganu, Selangor, Kelantan or Klang, and is used as evidence of the national pattern the territory stands under.

Human Rights Watch's federal-territory Sharia finding is stated for Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya and is not extended to Labuan. Whether Labuan's own Sharia enactment contains a cross-dressing offence is unresolved on the sources available here.

How Labuan immigration, port police or the courts treat a gender marker that does not match presentation is not sourced, nor is any outcome of a gender-mismatch check at entry.

The sources do not record any hate-crime provision, complaint mechanism or shelter in Labuan available to a transgender visitor, and no record exists of Labuan-specific sentencing under sections 377A or 377B.
